data-href="higgsfield-explore-masonry">html:has([data-explore-layout]) {
  scroll-behavior: auto;
}

[data-explore-layout] {
  container-type: inline-size;
  overflow-anchor: none;
  column-count: auto;
  --explore-columns: 2;
  --explore-gap: var(--spacing-q-400, 1rem);
  --explore-row-gap: var(--spacing-q-400, 1rem);
}

[data-explore-layout='2'] {
  --explore-gap: var(--spacing-q-200, 0.5rem);
}

[data-explore-layout='5'],
[data-explore-layout='6'] {
  --explore-gap: var(--spacing-q-200, 0.5rem);
  --explore-row-gap: var(--spacing-q-200, 0.5rem);
}

[data-explore-layout] > [data-explore-grid] {
  --explore-column-width: calc((100cqw - (var(--explore-columns) - 1) * var(--explore-gap)) / var(--explore-columns));
  position: relative;
  column-gap: var(--explore-gap);
  row-gap: var(--explore-row-gap);
  height: var(--explore-height-2);
}

[data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
  position: absolute;
  width: var(--explore-column-width);
  left: calc(var(--explore-x-2) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
  top: var(--explore-y-2);
}

@container (max-width: 24rem) {
  [data-explore-layout] > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 1;
    height: var(--explore-height-1);
  }

  [data-explore-layout] > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: 0;
    top: var(--explore-y-1);
  }
}

/* Three columns already in a narrow pane, where layout 4 would still show two. */
@container (min-width: 32rem) {
  [data-explore-layout='3'] > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 3;
    height: var(--explore-height-3);
  }

  [data-explore-layout='3'] > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: calc(var(--explore-x-3) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
    top: var(--explore-y-3);
  }
}

@container (min-width: 40rem) {
  :is([data-explore-layout='4'], [data-explore-layout='5'], [data-explore-layout='6']) > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 3;
    height: var(--explore-height-3);
  }

  :is([data-explore-layout='4'], [data-explore-layout='5'], [data-explore-layout='6']) > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: calc(var(--explore-x-3) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
    top: var(--explore-y-3);
  }
}

@container (min-width: 64rem) {
  [data-explore-layout='4'] > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 4;
    height: var(--explore-height-4);
  }

  [data-explore-layout='5'] > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 5;
    height: var(--explore-height-5);
  }

  [data-explore-layout='4'] > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: calc(var(--explore-x-4) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
    top: var(--explore-y-4);
  }

  [data-explore-layout='5'] > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: calc(var(--explore-x-5) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
    top: var(--explore-y-5);
  }
}

/* The home's six columns, from the xl container width; below it the 40rem rule keeps three. */
@container (min-width: 72rem) {
  [data-explore-layout='6'] > [data-explore-grid] {
    --explore-columns: 6;
    height: var(--explore-height-6);
  }

  [data-explore-layout='6'] > [data-explore-grid] > [data-explore-item] {
    left: calc(var(--explore-x-6) * (var(--explore-column-width) + var(--explore-gap)));
    top: var(--explore-y-6);
  }
}

From Roman stone carvers to newspaper printers, every era chose it. It's the favorite for building luxury brands, and a famous online test found 45,000 readers believed a serif more. But why? Do we really know?\n\nWelcome to Chapter 1 of 7 of my new series, Typecast, where we break down the psychology and semiotics of a typeface and how it makes or breaks a brand. No font conspiracy theories. Okay, first I need to explain something. Psychology and semiotics are not the same.\n\nThe psychology of type is about perception. How a human receives and reads letter shapes through the nervous system. In other words, perception, human, brain, interpretation. Serifs usually mean tradition, trust, authority, and elegance. But careful, like any font, that changes depending on weight and contrast.\n\nA thin, high-contrast serif isn't a chunky slab, both are serifs, with totally different meanings. One says luxury, the other, strength, and the old west. So saying serifs just mean trust is staying on the surface. Semiotics, though, is about signs. What's available to your eyes?\n\nMeaning what we see, what we perceive, and what it makes us think. And serifs feel trustworthy because we've seen them all our lives, on stone carvings and old dictionaries. Talking about serifs means talking about permanence and memory. Serifs are also tied to storytelling.\n\nThat's why almost every novel you've ever read is set in one. Like this one, or this one. That's why so many brands use a serif as the backbone of their identity. A serif is a font of solid promises. From Roman stone carvers to newspaper printers, every era chose it. It's the favorite for building luxury brands, and a famous online test found 45,000 readers believed a serif more. But why? Do we really know?\n\nWelcome to Chapter 1 of 7 of my new series, Typecast, where we break down the psychology and semiotics of a typeface and how it makes or breaks a brand. No font conspiracy theories. Okay, first I need to explain something. Psychology and semiotics are not the same.\n\nThe psychology of type is about perception. How a human receives and reads letter shapes through the nervous system. In other words, perception, human, brain, interpretation. Serifs usually mean tradition, trust, authority, and elegance. But careful, like any font, that changes depending on weight and contrast.\n\nA thin, high-contrast serif isn't a chunky slab, both are serifs, with totally different meanings. One says luxury, the other, strength, and the old west. So saying serifs just mean trust is staying on the surface. Semiotics, though, is about signs. What's available to your eyes?\n\nMeaning what we see, what we perceive, and what it makes us think. And serifs feel trustworthy because we've seen them all our lives, on stone carvings and old dictionaries. Talking about serifs means talking about permanence and memory. Serifs are also tied to storytelling.\n\nThat's why almost every novel you've ever read is set in one. Like this one, or this one. That's why so many brands use a serif as the backbone of their identity. A serif is a font of solid promises.
